subtopic: Frontend in a large team scale.
question: How do you manage a large frontend codebase with hundreds of developers to avoid conflicts and ensure efficiency?
expectedPoints: Explain codebase modularization
Discuss version control strategies
Describe communication and collaboration tools
Mention code review processes
Highlight continuous integration practices
followUps: What tools do you recommend for managing dependencies?
How do you handle code conflicts in a large team?
childExplanation: Imagine you and all your friends are building a giant LEGO city together. To make sure everyone can build their part without bumping into each other, you decide on rules and sections for each person. This way, everyone can work at the same time without messing up each other's work.
detailedExplanation:
Modular Architecture — Module Boundaries and Dependency Graphs

In a codebase with hundreds of developers, the first line of defense is a strict module boundary system. Use ESLint import/no-restricted-paths to enforce that @team-a/components cannot import from @team-b/internal — only from @team-b/public. Define a dependency graph using tools like nx graph or turborepo graph to visualize and enforce acyclic dependencies. Each module exposes a package.json with explicit exports field (Node.js 12.7+):

{
  "name": "@team-a/shared",
  "exports": {
    ".": "./src/index.ts",
    "./hooks": "./src/hooks/index.ts",
    "./components": "./src/components/index.ts",
    "./internal/*": null
  }
}

This prevents accidental deep imports. For a monorepo with 500+ packages, run nx affected:test on every PR — this detects which packages are impacted by a change and runs only their tests, reducing CI time from 45 minutes to under 4 minutes for typical changes.

Version Control Strategy — Trunk-Based Development with Feature Flags

For 100+ developers, long-lived branches create merge hell. Use trunk-based development: all developers commit to main multiple times per day. Feature work is hidden behind feature flags (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, or a custom @feature-flags package). A feature flag is a boolean check:

import { useFlag } from '@feature-flags/react';
function NewCheckout() {
  const isEnabled = useFlag('checkout-v2', { default: false });
  return isEnabled ? <CheckoutV2 /> : <CheckoutV1 />;
}

Flags are toggled via a centralized dashboard. This eliminates the need for feature branches: code is merged incrementally, and the flag is flipped when ready. For rollback, just toggle the flag off — no revert PR needed. Typical flag evaluation latency: <5 ms via a local cache (localStorage + in-memory map) synced every 30 seconds from the API.

Code Ownership and PR Automation

Use CODEOWNERS files (GitHub, GitLab) to require approval from the owning team for changes to specific paths. For example:

# CODEOWNERS
/packages/checkout/ @team-checkout
/packages/shared/design-system/ @team-design
/packages/shared/design-system/internal/* @team-design # no one else can touch internals

Automate PR creation for shared dependency updates using Renovate or Dependabot. For a design system update affecting 10 teams, Renovate creates 10 PRs simultaneously, each with a changelog and migration guide. Each team's CI runs visual regression tests (Chromatic) — if a team's UI diff is unexpected, they can block the merge. Track adoption via a dashboard showing which teams are on which version of @shared/design-system.

Contract Testing and API Boundaries

When teams share code through internal packages, use contract testing to prevent breaking changes. Each package publishes a type contract (TypeScript types + runtime validation with Zod or io-ts). The consumer's CI runs a contract test that imports the provider's contract and validates that the consumer's usage still matches. Example with Zod:

// @team-checkout/contracts
import { z } from 'zod';
export const CheckoutPayload = z.object({
  items: z.array(z.object({ sku: z.string(), quantity: z.number().min(1) })),
  coupon: z.string().optional(),
});
export type CheckoutPayload = z.infer<typeof CheckoutPayload>;

// @team-payments consumer
import { CheckoutPayload } from '@team-checkout/contracts';
// CI runs: CheckoutPayload.parse(sampleData) — fails if shape changed

This catches breaking changes at CI time, not at runtime. For shared components, use Storybook interaction tests + Chromatic visual diffs — any change to a shared component triggers a visual diff in all consuming stories.

⚠ Common Pitfall

Not enforcing module boundaries at the build level. ESLint rules are bypassable (someone can disable the rule). Use TypeScript path aliases with paths in tsconfig.json that map to the public API only, combined with a build-time check (e.g., a custom Rollup plugin that fails if an import resolves to a /**/internal/** path).

Senior signal: In a 100+ developer monorepo, the real bottleneck isn't merge conflicts — it's cognitive load. Each developer must understand only the public API of 3–5 modules, not the entire codebase. Enforce this with a dependency graph linter (e.g., dependency-cruiser) that fails CI if a module's fan-in exceeds 10 (too many consumers) or fan-out exceeds 5 (too many dependencies). This keeps the graph shallow and the mental model manageable.
🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1How does nx affected compute which packages are affected by a change?
    nx computes a project graph from project.json files and import statements. On each PR, it diffs the file tree against the base branch (e.g., main). It then walks the dependency graph from the changed files outward: any package that transitively depends on a changed file is marked as affected. This is done in O(N) time using a topological sort. For a 500-package repo, this takes ~200 ms.
  2. 2What happens when two teams simultaneously change the same shared component's public API?
    The first PR to merge wins. The second PR must rebase and resolve conflicts. To reduce this, enforce a breaking change policy: any public API change requires a major version bump and a migration period (e.g., 2 weeks) where both old and new APIs coexist. Use deprecation warnings (console.warn with a link to migration guide) for 2 weeks before removal. This gives downstream teams time to adapt.
  3. 3How do you handle a scenario where a shared component's visual change breaks 5 teams' UIs?
    First, the PR author runs nx affected:chromatic which generates visual diffs for all consuming stories. If any diff is unexpected, the PR is blocked. The author then either reverts the change or coordinates with each affected team. For large-scale changes, use a feature flag on the component itself: <Button variant="new" /> vs <Button variant="old" />. Teams opt-in by toggling the flag. After all teams migrate, remove the old variant.
  4. 4How do you prevent a team from accidentally introducing a circular dependency between packages?
    Use dependency-cruiser with a .dependency-cruiser.js config that defines forbidden rules: e.g., from: { path: '^packages/checkout' }, to: { path: '^packages/payments' } if checkout must not depend on payments. Run it as a pre-commit hook and in CI. For circular dependencies, the tool detects cycles and fails. The fix is to extract the shared logic into a new package that both depend on, or use dependency inversion (the consumer defines an interface, the provider implements it).
  5. 5How do you measure and improve developer productivity in a large monorepo?
    Track cycle time (time from first commit to merge), CI failure rate, and time to first green CI. Use DORA metrics: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, mean time to recovery (MTTR), change failure rate. For the monorepo itself, measure cold build time (full build from scratch) and incremental build time (after a single file change). Target: cold build <5 minutes, incremental <10 seconds. Use remote caching (nx cloud, turborepo remote cache) to share build artifacts across developers — this reduces a 5-minute cold build to 30 seconds for a new developer.

question: What are the trade-offs between using a monorepo and a polyrepo in frontend system design?
expectedPoints: Ease of code sharing and updates
Synchronization of changes across projects
Complexity of build/CI processes
Team boundaries and ownership clarity
followUps: How do tools like Nx or Turborepo assist in monorepo management?
What challenges might arise with versioning in a polyrepo setup?
childExplanation: Imagine you have a big box of toys (monorepo) where you can easily find and play with any toy, but you need to keep it organized. Or, you have separate smaller boxes (polyrepo) for different toys, which makes it easier to find a specific type of toy, but you might need to open many boxes to play with them all together.
detailedExplanation:
Monorepo vs Polyrepo — Core Trade-offs

A monorepo stores all frontend projects (apps, shared UI libraries, configs) in a single Git repository. A polyrepo uses separate repositories per project or component. The fundamental trade-off is coordination cost vs. independence. Monorepos excel at cross-project refactoring — a single commit can update an API contract across 50 packages — but require sophisticated build orchestration. Polyrepos give teams full autonomy but force shared code through published packages (npm, publishConfig), introducing versioning overhead and multi-PR synchronization.

Key metrics: monorepo CI times can be 40–60% faster than polyrepo for equivalent changes when using incremental builds (Nx, Turborepo). Polyrepo clone times are ~200ms per repo vs. 2–5 minutes for a monorepo with 10+ years of history. Monorepo storage can reach 2–5 GB; polyrepo averages 100–500 MB per repo.

Build and CI Complexity

Monorepos require affected project detection to avoid rebuilding everything. Tools like Nx compute a dependency graph and only rebuild packages whose source changed. Example configuration:

// nx.json — monorepo build orchestration
{
  "tasksRunnerOptions": {
    "default": {
      "runner": "nx/tasks-runners/default",
      "options": {
        "cacheableOperations": ["build", "test", "lint"],
        "cacheDirectory": ".nx-cache",
        "remoteCache": { "enabled": true }
      }
    }
  },
  "targetDefaults": {
    "build": { "dependsOn": ["^build"] },
    "test": { "dependsOn": ["build"] }
  }
}

Polyrepos avoid this complexity — each repo has its own package.json and CI pipeline. However, cross-repo changes require multiple PRs and releases. A shared component update might need: PR in ui-lib → publish v2.0.0 → PR in app-a to upgrade → PR in app-b to upgrade. This cycle adds 30–60 minutes of overhead per change.

Code Sharing and Versioning Strategies

In monorepos, packages can import each other directly via TypeScript path aliases (@myorg/ui → packages/ui/src). This eliminates the need for npm publish during development. Versioning is managed centrally with single version policy (all packages share the same dependency version) or independent versioning (each package tracks its own).

Polyrepos rely on npm workspaces or pnpm catalogs for local development, but published packages require semantic versioning. A common pattern:

// pnpm-workspace.yaml — polyrepo with local linking
packages:
  - 'packages/*'
  - 'apps/*'
catalog:
  react: ^18.2.0
  typescript: ^5.4.0

Polyrepo teams often use changesets (@changesets/cli) to automate version bumps and changelogs. Each PR includes a changeset file describing the semver bump (major/minor/patch). On merge, a bot creates a release PR. This adds ~5 minutes per PR but ensures version consistency.

Team Boundaries and Ownership

Monorepos require explicit ownership via CODEOWNERS files. Example:

# .github/CODEOWNERS
/packages/shared-ui/ @team-design-system
/apps/dashboard/ @team-dashboard
/apps/mobile/ @team-mobile
*.config.js @team-platform

Without this, teams can accidentally modify each other's code. Polyrepos enforce ownership by repository — only @team-dashboard can merge to dashboard-repo. However, this creates silos: a design system change requires the design team to publish a new version, then each consumer team updates independently. This can take 2–5 days for a simple button style change vs. 30 minutes in a monorepo.

⚠ Common Pitfall

In a monorepo, teams often forget to configure CODEOWNERS for shared config files (tsconfig.json, .eslintrc.js). This leads to conflicting PRs where one team changes the TypeScript strictness and another team's build breaks. Always set CODEOWNERS for root-level configs to a platform team.

Senior signal: The choice between monorepo and polyrepo is not binary — many organizations adopt a hybrid approach: a monorepo for tightly coupled frontend apps (dashboard, admin, public site) and separate polyrepos for truly independent products (mobile app, third-party SDK). The key metric is cross-project change frequency: if more than 20% of commits touch multiple projects, a monorepo is likely better. Measure this with git log --oneline --name-only over 3 months.
🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1How does Nx compute the dependency graph for affected project detection?
    Nx parses package.json, tsconfig.json paths, and import statements to build a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of project dependencies. On each commit, it compares the current file tree against the last successful build's tree (stored in .nx-cache). Only projects whose files changed, or whose dependencies changed, are marked as "affected." The nx affected:build command then runs builds only for those projects. This reduces CI time from 30 minutes to 3–5 minutes for a 100-package monorepo.
  2. 2What are the trade-offs of using pnpm workspaces with catalog protocol vs. npm workspaces for dependency management?
    pnpm's catalog: protocol enforces a single version of a dependency across all packages, preventing diamond dependency conflicts. npm workspaces allow per-package overrides, which can lead to multiple versions of the same dependency (e.g., React 18.2.0 in one package, 18.3.0 in another). pnpm's strict mode also prevents packages from accessing dependencies not listed in their package.json, catching missing dependency bugs at install time. The cost: pnpm's symlink-based node_modules structure can confuse some tools (e.g., Jest module resolution requires moduleNameMapper configuration).
  3. 3How do you handle a breaking change in a shared library that affects 20+ consuming apps in a monorepo?
    Use a codemod approach: write a jscodeshift script that automatically updates all consumers. Run it as part of the PR that introduces the breaking change. The PR should include: (1) the library change, (2) the codemod, (3) all consumer updates applied by the codemod. Nx's nx affected:test will run tests for all 20+ apps. If any fail, the PR is blocked. This ensures zero regressions. Without a codemod, the PR would require manual updates across 20+ apps, taking 2–3 days instead of 30 minutes.
  4. 4What happens when two teams in a monorepo have conflicting TypeScript strictness settings?
    Each package can override tsconfig.json via extends. Team A's package can set "strict": true, Team B's can set "strict": false. The root tsconfig.json should define the minimum baseline (e.g., "noImplicitAny": true). The danger: if Team A's package is a dependency of Team B's, TypeScript will use Team A's strict settings when compiling Team B's code that imports from A. This can cause unexpected type errors. Solution: use project references with composite: true to isolate compilation boundaries.
  5. 5How would you design a CI pipeline that supports both monorepo and polyrepo workflows for a team transitioning between the two?
    Use a modular CI architecture with shared actions/composites. Each repository (mono or poly) defines a .github/workflows/ci.yml that calls reusable actions: setup-node, install-deps, lint, test, build. For monorepos, add an affected step that computes which projects to process. For polyrepos, skip that step. Use concurrency groups to cancel redundant runs. Key metrics: keep CI under 10 minutes for 95% of PRs. Monitor cache hit rate (target >80%) and build time per project (target <2 minutes).

question: How would you design a real-time chat application focusing on scalability and performance?
expectedPoints: Selects WebSockets for full-duplex real-time messaging; knows when SSE or polling is acceptable.
Explains message delivery guarantees: at-least-once with client-side deduplication by message ID.
Handles optimistic UI: message appears sent instantly, then confirmed or rolled back on ack/error.
Designs typing indicators and presence (online/offline) as ephemeral state separate from message persistence.
Addresses offline support: queue outbound messages in IndexedDB, sync on reconnect.
Discusses scaling: sticky sessions or pub/sub (Redis) to fan-out messages across server nodes.
followUps: How do you guarantee message ordering when the client and server are on different timezones?
How would you implement read receipts (double-tick pattern) without overloading the server?
What happens to queued messages when a WebSocket connection drops mid-send?
How would you design the chat UI to stay responsive while receiving 100+ messages/second in a group chat?
How do you handle message search — full-text search on a potentially huge message history?
Walk me through designing end-to-end encryption for a chat app.
childExplanation: Imagine you have a walkie-talkie that lets you talk to your friend instantly. A chat app works like that, but on your phone. It needs to be fast, even if you have a lot of friends talking at once.
detailedExplanation:
Interview Framework — Clarify First

Before architecting, ask: (1) 1:1 only or group chats? (2) Maximum group size? (3) Message history retention? (4) File/media sharing? (5) E2E encryption required? These change the design significantly. Then frame your answer around: transport layer → message flow → delivery guarantees → offline → presence.

Transport: WebSockets vs SSE vs Polling

  • WebSockets: full-duplex, persistent TCP — ideal for chat. Single connection per client; server can push any time. Use wss:// (TLS) always.
  • SSE (Server-Sent Events): server→client only over HTTP. Good for notification feeds but forces HTTP requests for sends — adds latency.
  • Long-polling: last resort; works behind proxies that block WS. Higher server load, ~1 s latency floor.

Connection management: implement exponential back-off reconnect (1 s → 2 s → 4 s → max 30 s) with jitter. On reconnect, send the client's last-seen sequence number so the server replays missed messages.

Message Flow and Delivery Guarantees

Target: at-least-once delivery with client-side deduplication.

  1. Client sends message with a client-generated UUID (clientMsgId).
  2. Server persists to DB, assigns a server sequence number, broadcasts to all participants via pub/sub (e.g., Redis).
  3. Server sends ACK back to sender with { clientMsgId, serverMsgId, timestamp }.
  4. If no ACK within 5 s, client retries. Server deduplicates on clientMsgId — idempotent insert.
  5. Recipients acknowledge receipt; sender UI upgrades from "sent ✓" to "delivered ✓✓".
⚠ Common Pitfall

Using insertion timestamp as message ordering key. Clock skew between clients causes visible message reordering. Use a server-assigned monotonic sequence number per conversation instead.

Optimistic UI

Don't wait for the server round-trip before showing the message. Render it immediately in a "pending" state (e.g., grey text, clock icon). On ACK: transition to confirmed state. On error: show retry button and mark failed. Store pending messages in component state (or Zustand/Redux) keyed by clientMsgId.

Typing Indicators and Presence

These are ephemeral state — never persist to the primary DB.

  • Typing: throttle client emit to once per 1–2 s while composing. Server broadcasts { userId, conversationId, typing: true }. Recipient sets a 3 s timeout; if no new typing event arrives, clear the indicator.
  • Online/Offline presence: track WebSocket connection count per user in Redis (INCR on connect, DECR on disconnect). Broadcast status change to relevant users. Use a heartbeat ping (every 25 s) to detect stale connections that didn't clean up.

Offline Support

  • Outbound queue: when offline, write messages to IndexedDB with pending status. On reconnect, drain the queue sequentially.
  • Inbound sync: on reconnect, send { lastSeenSeq }; server returns missed messages in a batch. Merge into local message store, deduplicate by serverMsgId.
  • Service Worker: cache the app shell so the UI loads offline; intercept API calls and serve cached message list for read-only access.

Scaling

A single WebSocket server can handle ~10k–100k concurrent connections. Beyond that, use sticky sessions at the load balancer + Redis pub/sub to fan-out messages across nodes. When User A (on server-1) sends to User B (on server-2), server-1 publishes to Redis channel conversation:{id}, and server-2 (subscribed) pushes to User B's socket.

Senior signal: mention that typing indicators and presence should go through a separate lightweight channel (or even a dedicated presence service) rather than the message persistence pipeline — they have very different durability and throughput characteristics.
🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1How do you handle message ordering across clients with clock skew?
    Never trust client timestamps for ordering. Assign a server-side monotonic sequence number per conversation (or use a Lamport clock). Each message record stores serverSeq INT NOT NULL and clients sort by serverSeq ascending. Display the client-formatted timestamp (for human readability) but order by serverSeq. For distributed servers, a global sequence generator (e.g., Snowflake ID, or a Redis INCR per conversation) ensures total ordering without a single DB bottleneck.
  2. 2How would you implement read receipts efficiently at scale?
    Naive approach (ACK per message) floods the server in group chats. Better: track a lastReadSeq cursor per user per conversation. When a user views the conversation, send a single READ { conversationId, upToSeq } event. The server updates lastReadSeq and fan-outs to other participants. The sender UI recalculates receipt state by comparing each message's serverSeq to each participant's lastReadSeq. One event covers all messages up to that point rather than N individual ACKs.
  3. 3How do you keep the message list performant in a group chat with thousands of messages?
    Use a virtualised list (react-window or tanstack/virtual) — only render the messages visible in the viewport plus a small overscan buffer. Variable-height rows require measuring rendered height per message and caching it. Load history in pages (cursor-based pagination by serverSeq). When the user scrolls up past the first loaded message, fetch the previous page and prepend — preserve scroll position by adjusting scrollTop to compensate for the newly added height at the top.
  4. 4Walk through WebSocket reconnection and missed-message recovery.
    (1) Connection drops — client detects via close event or heartbeat timeout. (2) Client queues outbound messages to IndexedDB. (3) Exponential back-off reconnect: 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, 8 s, max 30 s. Add ±30% jitter to prevent thundering herd after a server restart. (4) On reconnect, client sends { lastSeenSeq } for each active conversation. (5) Server queries messages with serverSeq > lastSeenSeq, returns batch. (6) Client merges batch, deduplicates, re-renders. (7) Drain the outbound queue — retry pending messages sequentially.
  5. 5How would you add end-to-end encryption without breaking server-side features like search or push notifications?
    E2E encryption means the server stores ciphertext — it cannot read message content. This breaks: server-side search (solve with client-side search over decrypted local store), push notification previews (send an encrypted payload; the client decrypts on-device via the Notification API in a Service Worker), and backup/recovery (export encrypted key bundle to user's cloud storage). Key exchange: use the Signal Protocol (Double Ratchet + X3DH) — widely battle-tested. Each device generates an identity key pair; the server stores only public keys. A sending client fetches the recipient's public key bundle from the server and derives a shared secret without the server ever seeing it.

question: How would you design a chat application to handle both 1-1 and group messaging with low latency?
expectedPoints: Explain handling of 1-1 and group messaging.
Discuss strategies for ensuring low latency.
Describe how to maintain message history.
Explain handling of network disruptions.
Discuss UI/UX considerations for smooth scrolling.
followUps: How would you ensure message delivery in poor network conditions?
What strategies would you use to optimize for low latency?
childExplanation: Imagine you have a walkie-talkie that lets you talk to one friend or a group of friends. You need to make sure everyone hears you quickly and clearly, even if you're in a noisy place or moving around.
detailedExplanation:
WebSocket Connection Management and Reconnection Strategy

For low-latency chat, WebSockets are the standard transport. The initial handshake uses HTTP/1.1 Upgrade or HTTP/2 CONNECT. Once established, the connection must survive network blips. Implement a staggered exponential backoff reconnection strategy: initial delay 1s, then 2s, 4s, 8s, capped at 30s. Use navigator.onLine and window.addEventListener('online', ...) to detect connectivity restoration and trigger immediate reconnect. The WebSocket URL should include a sessionId query parameter for server-side state recovery.

class ChatSocket {
  constructor(url, sessionId) {
    this.url = `${url}?sessionId=${sessionId}`;
    this.reconnectDelay = 1000;
    this.maxDelay = 30000;
    this.connect();
  }
  connect() {
    this.ws = new WebSocket(this.url);
    this.ws.onopen = () => { this.reconnectDelay = 1000; };
    this.ws.onclose = (e) => {
      if (e.code !== 1000) this.scheduleReconnect();
    };
    this.ws.onmessage = (e) => this.handleMessage(JSON.parse(e.data));
  }
  scheduleReconnect() {
    setTimeout(() => this.connect(), this.reconnectDelay);
    this.reconnectDelay = Math.min(this.reconnectDelay * 2, this.maxDelay);
  }
}

Fan-Out Architecture for Group Messages

For group chats, a single message must be delivered to all members. Two strategies: fan-out on write (push message to each member's inbox) or fan-out on read (pull from a shared group timeline). For groups <100 members, fan-out on write is preferred for low latency — the server writes one copy per member to a per-user message queue (stored in Redis sorted sets keyed by user:{userId}:inbox). For groups >100 members, fan-out on read is more efficient: write once to a group timeline (group:{groupId}:timeline) and each client fetches from there with a lastSeenId cursor. Hybrid approach: use fan-out on write for groups <50, fan-out on read for larger groups, with a threshold configurable per workspace.

Message Ordering and Deduplication

Each message gets a Lamport timestamp (logical clock) for causal ordering across clients. The server assigns a monotonically increasing serverId (64-bit integer) upon receipt. Clients sort by serverId for display order. For deduplication, the client generates a clientMsgId (UUID v4, 36 bytes) before sending. The server stores clientMsgId in a Redis set with TTL 24h. If a duplicate clientMsgId arrives (from retry), the server returns the stored serverId without re-processing. The client uses serverId to update the message status from "sending" to "sent".

// Client-side message sending with retry
async function sendMessage(text, chatId) {
  const clientMsgId = crypto.randomUUID();
  const msg = { clientMsgId, chatId, text, timestamp: Date.now() };
  // Optimistic UI update
  addMessageToUI({ ...msg, status: 'sending' });
  let retries = 0;
  while (retries < 3) {
    try {
      const res = await ws.send(JSON.stringify(msg));
      const { serverId } = await waitForAck(clientMsgId);
      updateMessageStatus(clientMsgId, 'sent', serverId);
      return;
    } catch {
      retries++;
      await sleep(1000 * Math.pow(2, retries));
    }
  }
  updateMessageStatus(clientMsgId, 'failed');
}

Offline Message Sync and State Reconciliation

When a client reconnects after being offline, it must sync missed messages. The client stores the lastReceivedServerId locally (IndexedDB for web, SQLite for mobile). On reconnect, it sends a sync message with lastReceivedServerId. The server returns all messages with serverId > lastReceivedServerId from the user's inbox (for fan-out on write) or from all group timelines the user belongs to (for fan-out on read). For large gaps (>1000 messages), the server paginates: first batch of 100 messages, then the client requests the next batch. The sync endpoint must complete within 500ms for 95th percentile to avoid blocking the UI. Use Promise.all to fetch from multiple group timelines concurrently.

⚠ Common Pitfall

Assuming WebSocket messages arrive in order. Network proxies and load balancers can reorder frames. Always include a serverId or sequence number in each message and sort client-side before rendering. Never rely on Array.push() order from onmessage.

Senior signal: For group chats with >1000 members, implement a presence-based fan-out filter — only deliver messages to members who are currently online (tracked via WebSocket heartbeat every 30s). Offline members fetch via sync on reconnect. This reduces write amplification from O(n) to O(activeUsers) and cuts server CPU by 60-80% for large groups.
🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1How does the server detect and handle duplicate WebSocket connections from the same user?
    The server maintains a Map<userId, WebSocket>. When a new connection arrives with the same userId, the server closes the old connection with code 1001 (Going Away) and replaces it with the new one. This prevents duplicate message delivery. The old connection's pending messages are drained and re-queued for the new socket. A 2-second grace period allows the client to re-establish before flushing the old socket's buffer.
  2. 2What data structure is used for the per-user inbox in fan-out on write, and how is it garbage collected?
    A Redis sorted set with serverId as score and message JSON as value. Messages are evicted after 30 days via a TTL on the key, or when the set exceeds 10,000 entries (oldest removed via ZREMRANGEBYRANK). For active users, messages are consumed on delivery and removed immediately. For inactive users, a background job scans and trims daily. The set is sharded by userId % 1024 to avoid hot keys.
  3. 3How do you handle the case where a user sends a message while offline and the group has >100 members (fan-out on read)?
    The client queues the message locally in IndexedDB with clientMsgId and a queuedAt timestamp. On reconnect, it sends all queued messages in order. The server writes the message to the group timeline and returns serverId. The client then updates the local message status. If the group timeline has advanced significantly (e.g., 5000 messages ahead), the client must fetch the gap first to maintain ordering — the server includes a gapStartServerId in the response, and the client fetches missing messages before displaying the sent message.
  4. 4How do you ensure read receipts are accurate when the client is offline?
    The client stores the lastReadServerId per chat in IndexedDB. On reconnect, it sends a batch of readReceipt events for all chats where lastReadServerId advanced. The server updates a Redis hash chat:{chatId}:readReceipts with { userId: lastReadServerId }. For group chats, the server broadcasts the updated read receipt to other online members via WebSocket. To avoid storms on reconnect, the client debounces read receipt updates to once per 5 seconds per chat.
  5. 5How would you design the system to support end-to-end encryption (E2EE) without breaking the fan-out architecture?
    Each group has a shared symmetric key (AES-256-GCM) stored in the server as encrypted blobs per member (encrypted with each member's public key). When a message is sent, the client encrypts the payload with the group key. The server stores the encrypted ciphertext in the timeline/inbox. For fan-out on write, the server writes the same ciphertext to each inbox — no per-member encryption needed. Key rotation happens when a member leaves: the server generates a new group key, encrypts it for remaining members, and broadcasts a key change message. The client must re-encrypt the last 100 messages with the new key for forward secrecy. This adds ~50ms latency per message for encryption/decryption on modern devices.

question: How would you design an autocomplete component to handle debounce and race conditions?
expectedPoints: Implements debounce (150–300 ms) to reduce API calls; understands the difference from throttle.
Fixes race conditions with AbortController — cancels stale in-flight requests when a newer keystroke fires.
Layers a client-side cache (Map keyed by prefix) to avoid re-fetching results for previously seen queries.
Builds full keyboard navigation (↑↓ to move, Enter to select, Esc to close) with ARIA (role=combobox, aria-activedescendant).
Considers UX details: highlight the matched substring in results, show loading state, handle empty state gracefully.
Discusses virtualisation for large result lists and whether to fetch from CDN edge for ultra-low latency.
followUps: What is the difference between debounce and throttle — when would you use throttle for autocomplete?
How would you handle a search that requires authentication vs one that's public and cacheable on a CDN?
How do you design the server-side autocomplete index for sub-50 ms response times?
How would you track which suggestions users actually click to improve ranking over time?
What accessibility role and attribute changes does the dropdown need when the list updates?
How would you support fuzzy matching (tolerating typos) client-side without a round-trip?
childExplanation: Imagine you're typing in a search box and it suggests words as you type. To make sure it works well, we need to make it wait a bit before searching, so it doesn't search too much. We also need to make sure it doesn't get confused if you type fast.
detailedExplanation:
Interview Framework

Scope the problem: single-field search or multi-context (e.g., users, repos, files)? Backend-powered or client-side only? Max suggestions shown? Then structure your answer: input handling → network → cache → rendering → accessibility.

Debounce — The First Layer of Defence

Fire the API request only after the user pauses typing. Typical delay: 150–300 ms (lower feels more responsive; higher saves API calls).

  • Debounce: reset the timer on every keystroke; fire once after silence. Right for search — you want the result after the user finishes a thought.
  • Throttle: fire at most once per interval regardless of activity. Right for scroll/resize handlers, not ideal here — first keystroke waits unnecessarily.

Implementation pattern with useRef to survive re-renders:

const timer = useRef();
function handleChange(val) {
  clearTimeout(timer.current);
  timer.current = setTimeout(() => fetchSuggestions(val), 250);
}

Race Conditions — AbortController

User types "re" (request A fires) then immediately "rea" (request B fires). If A is slower than B and arrives last, stale results overwrite fresh ones.

Fix: cancel the previous in-flight request with AbortController:

const ctrlRef = useRef();
async function fetchSuggestions(query) {
  ctrlRef.current?.abort();
  ctrlRef.current = new AbortController();
  const res = await fetch(`/api/suggest?q=${query}`, {
    signal: ctrlRef.current.signal
  });
  setSuggestions(await res.json());
}

Catch AbortError separately to avoid showing an error state for cancelled requests.

Client-Side Cache

Results for the same prefix rarely change within a session. Keep a Map<string, Suggestion[]> in a useRef. Before fetching, check the map — return cached result instantly (zero latency, zero API cost). Cap the map at ~100 entries and evict LRU to avoid memory growth on long sessions.

Keyboard Navigation and ARIA

ARIA pattern: role="combobox" on the input, role="listbox" on the dropdown, role="option" on each item, aria-activedescendant on the input pointing to the focused option's ID, aria-expanded reflects open/closed state.

  • ↓ — move focus to next item (wrap at bottom to input)
  • ↑ — move focus to previous (wrap at top to input)
  • Enter — select focused item or submit current input
  • Escape — close dropdown, return focus to input
  • Tab — close dropdown, move to next focusable element
⚠ Common Pitfall

Moving DOM focus into the list items breaks the input for screen readers. Instead, keep DOM focus on the input and use aria-activedescendant to announce the visually highlighted item. Screen readers announce the item text without moving the keyboard cursor out of the input.

Result Rendering and UX Details

  • Highlight matched substring: split result text on the query string, wrap matched part in <mark>.
  • Loading state: show a spinner or skeleton after debounce fires but before the response arrives — typically 50–200 ms window.
  • Empty state: distinguish "no results" from "still loading" — show "No results for X" only after a response with empty array.
  • Virtualise long lists: cap displayed results at 8–10 for usability.
Senior signal: mention that autocomplete suggestions for public search boxes can be served from a CDN edge function (Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge) for <10 ms response time globally, since the index is read-only and prefix-keyed.
🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1Why does AbortController not fully solve race conditions — what else is needed?
    AbortController cancels the network request, but if two requests somehow complete simultaneously (both from cache, or via a race in microtask ordering), the last setState call wins. The additional guard: tag each request with an incrementing requestId. In the response handler, only call setState if requestId === latestRequestId.current. This pattern (request ID guard) is belt-and-suspenders alongside AbortController.
  2. 2How would you design a server-side autocomplete endpoint for sub-50 ms P99 latency?
    Pre-compute a sorted prefix index in Redis (ZRANGEBYLEX on a sorted set works well for prefix search). Each key in the sorted set is a suggestion string with score 0; range query returns all strings between "prefix" and "prefixÿ". Weight results by frequency (query count) by encoding score as -frequency. For personalisation, blend global frequency with user-specific recency signals. Keep the index in RAM (Redis), respond directly from the edge function — no DB query needed.
  3. 3How would you add fuzzy matching (typo tolerance) without a server round-trip?
    For small, bounded datasets (city names, product SKUs <10k items): download the full list on first load, cache in memory, and use a client-side fuzzy library (Fuse.js, minisearch) for instant offline matching. For large open-ended search: send the query to the server with a fuzzy=true flag. The server uses trigram indexing (PostgreSQL pg_trgm, Elasticsearch) to find results within edit distance 1–2. Client-side fuzzy + server-side prefix for hybrid: show instant fuzzy results from local cache while the server request is in flight; merge and deduplicate on arrival.
  4. 4How do you track and use click-through data to improve suggestion ranking?
    Log events: { query, suggestionRank, selectedSuggestion, userId, sessionId, timestamp }. Aggregate: compute click-through rate (CTR) per suggestion per prefix. Feed CTR into the ranking model — boost suggestions with higher CTR for that prefix. Also track "no-result searches" (query with zero selections) to identify gaps in the index. A/B test ranking changes: measure task completion rate (user found what they wanted) not just CTR.
  5. 5What ARIA attribute updates are needed when the suggestion list changes dynamically?
    When results arrive: set aria-expanded="true" on the combobox, update aria-controls to point to the listbox ID, set aria-setsize on each option to the total count, and aria-posinset to the item's 1-based position. A visually-hidden live region with aria-live="polite" announces "5 suggestions available". When the list is empty or hidden: aria-expanded="false". Clear aria-activedescendant when no item is highlighted.

question: How would you design a frontend system to handle user input efficiently with debounce and caching?
expectedPoints: Explain the role of debounce in handling input.
Describe how caching can improve performance.
Discuss the use of AbortController for managing fetch requests.
Explain how to ensure accessibility in dropdown rendering.
Address how to prevent race conditions with new input.
followUps: How would you handle a scenario where the cache is stale?
What are the trade-offs of using a longer debounce time?
childExplanation: Imagine you're trying to catch a ball, but you only want to catch the last one thrown. Debounce is like waiting a bit before you decide which ball to catch, and caching is like remembering which balls you've already caught so you don't have to catch them again.
detailedExplanation:
Debounce — Timing and Implementation Nuances

Debounce is the first line of defense against excessive function calls. The optimal delay depends on user expectation: 150–200 ms for search-as-you-type (feels instant), 300–400 ms for form validation (reduces false positives). Internally, debounce uses a closure with setTimeout and clearTimeout. The key is storing the timer reference in a useRef hook to survive React re-renders without resetting.

function useDebounce(callback, delay = 250) {
  const timerRef = useRef();
  const callbackRef = useRef(callback);
  useEffect(() => { callbackRef.current = callback; }, [callback]);

  return useCallback((...args) => {
    clearTimeout(timerRef.current);
    timerRef.current = setTimeout(() => {
      callbackRef.current(...args);
    }, delay);
  }, [delay]);
}

For leading-edge debounce (fire immediately, then debounce subsequent calls), use a flag: if (!timerRef.current) callbackRef.current(...args);. This is useful for "search on Enter" combined with debounced suggestions.

Caching Strategy — Stale-While-Revalidate and LRU

Caching prevents redundant network calls. Use a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache with a max size of 50–100 entries (bounded memory). Each entry stores: { value: results[], timestamp: number, ttl: number }. On cache hit, check TTL (e.g., 60 seconds). If stale, return cached value immediately and trigger a background refresh (stale-while-revalidate pattern).

class LRUCache {
  constructor(maxSize = 100) {
    this.maxSize = maxSize;
    this.cache = new Map();
  }
  get(key) {
    if (!this.cache.has(key)) return null;
    const entry = this.cache.get(key);
    this.cache.delete(key);
    this.cache.set(key, entry); // move to end (most recent)
    return entry;
  }
  set(key, value) {
    if (this.cache.has(key)) this.cache.delete(key);
    else if (this.cache.size >= this.maxSize) {
      const oldest = this.cache.keys().next().value;
      this.cache.delete(oldest);
    }
    this.cache.set(key, value);
  }
}

For server-side caching, use Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300 on the API response. The browser cache serves stale data for 5 minutes while revalidating in the background.

Race Condition Prevention — Request ID and AbortController

Even with AbortController, two requests can complete simultaneously if both are served from cache (microtask ordering). The robust solution: tag each request with an incrementing requestId and only update state if the response's requestId matches the latest.

const requestIdRef = useRef(0);
async function fetchWithRaceGuard(query) {
  const currentId = ++requestIdRef.current;
  ctrlRef.current?.abort();
  ctrlRef.current = new AbortController();
  try {
    const res = await fetch(`/api/suggest?q=${query}`, {
      signal: ctrlRef.current.signal
    });
    const data = await res.json();
    if (currentId === requestIdRef.current) {
      setSuggestions(data);
    }
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.name !== 'AbortError') {
      setError(err);
    }
  }
}

This pattern handles the edge case where AbortController fails (e.g., browser bug) or both requests complete from cache.

Rendering Performance — Virtualization and Memoization

For large suggestion lists (100+ items), use virtualization (react-window, react-virtuoso) to render only visible items. Each row height: 32–48 px. The virtual list container should have overflow-y: auto and a fixed height (e.g., max-height: 300px). Memoize the suggestion list with React.memo and useMemo to avoid re-renders when the input changes but results haven't.

const SuggestionList = React.memo(({ items, onSelect }) => {
  return (
    <ul role="listbox">
      {items.map((item, idx) => (
        <li key={item.id} role="option" aria-posinset={idx + 1} aria-setsize={items.length}>
          {item.label}
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
});

For keyboard navigation, use aria-activedescendant on the input to point to the currently highlighted option, keeping focus on the input.

⚠ Common Pitfall

Storing the entire suggestion list in React state without memoization causes the entire dropdown to re-render on every keystroke, even when the results haven't changed. Always compare previous and next results with a shallow equality check before updating state.

Senior signal: For high-traffic autocomplete (e.g., Google Search), the debounce delay should be adaptive — start with 150 ms, then increase to 300 ms if the user types faster than 5 characters per second (detected via performance.now() on each keystroke). This balances perceived responsiveness with server load.
🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1How does the LRU cache eviction policy interact with the stale-while-revalidate pattern — what happens when a stale entry is evicted before revalidation completes?
    If a stale entry is evicted, the background revalidation will still complete but the result is discarded. The next request for that key will miss the cache and fetch fresh data. To prevent this, extend the TTL of entries that are currently being revalidated (set a revalidating flag). Alternatively, use a two-tier cache: a small fast LRU for hot entries and a larger slower cache for cold entries.
  2. 2What are the memory implications of storing the entire suggestion list in the cache — how do you bound it?
    Each suggestion entry can be 200–500 bytes (JSON string). With 100 entries and 50 cached queries, that's ~2.5 MB — acceptable. But if each query returns 1000 suggestions (e.g., product catalog), that's 50 MB. Bound by: (1) limiting max suggestions per query to 20, (2) using a WeakMap for suggestion objects to allow garbage collection, (3) compressing strings with pako before storing.
  3. 3How do you handle the case where the user types a query that matches a cached result but the server data has changed — what's the staleness window?
    Use a staleTime of 30–60 seconds for autocomplete (data changes infrequently). For real-time data (stock prices), set staleTime: 0 and always fetch. The trade-off: longer stale time reduces server load but risks showing outdated results. Implement a "last updated" timestamp in the UI: Results from 45 seconds ago.
  4. 4What happens when the user types very fast (e.g., 20 characters in 1 second) — how does debounce interact with the AbortController?
    With a 250 ms debounce, only the last query fires. But if the user types "hello world" in 500 ms, the debounce fires once with "hello world". The AbortController cancels any previous in-flight request. However, if the user pauses mid-word (e.g., "hel" then 300 ms later "lo"), two requests fire sequentially. The request ID guard ensures only the latest response updates state.
  5. 5How would you design a system that supports both debounced search and instant search (e.g., pressing Enter) without race conditions?
    Maintain two separate request queues: one for debounced (timer-based) and one for instant (Enter key). Each queue has its own AbortController and requestId. On Enter, cancel the debounce timer and fire the instant request immediately. The instant request's requestId is higher than any pending debounced request, so it wins. After the instant response, reset the debounce timer to avoid double-fetching.

question: How do you handle race conditions in a search autocomplete feature?
expectedPoints: Use AbortController to cancel outdated requests
Implement caching for repeated queries
Use debounce to limit API requests
Ensure accessibility with ARIA attributes
Handle errors except 'AbortError'
followUps: What are the benefits of caching in search features?
How does debounce improve performance in autocomplete?
childExplanation: Imagine you're asking a friend to fetch you a book, but you change your mind and ask for a different one before they return. You need a way to tell them to ignore the first request. In programming, we use tools to cancel old requests when new ones come in, so we don't get the wrong book.
detailedExplanation:
Race Condition Taxonomy in Autocomplete

Race conditions in autocomplete fall into three categories, each requiring distinct mitigation. Stale response races occur when request A (query "re") and request B (query "rea") are dispatched sequentially, but A's response arrives after B's due to network variance — the user sees outdated results for "re" after typing "rea". Stale closure races happen in React when an event handler captures a stale query value from a previous render, then fires after the state has updated, operating on old data. Concurrent mutation races arise when two components or users modify the same cache entry or state slice simultaneously, causing one update to be lost. For autocomplete, the dominant threat is stale responses, which we solve with AbortController and request sequencing.

Debounce — Reducing Request Volume

Debounce delays the API call until the user pauses typing, typically 200–400 ms. A 300 ms debounce at 60 WPM typing reduces requests from ~10 per second to ~3 per second. Implementation uses useRef to persist the timer across re-renders:

const debounceTimer = useRef(null);
const DEBOUNCE_MS = 300;

function handleInput(value) {
  clearTimeout(debounceTimer.current);
  debounceTimer.current = setTimeout(() => {
    fetchSuggestions(value);
  }, DEBOUNCE_MS);
}

Throttle is inappropriate here — it fires at fixed intervals (e.g., every 200 ms), causing unnecessary requests during rapid typing and delaying the first response. Debounce aligns with user intent: fire after the user finishes a thought.

AbortController — Cancelling Stale Requests

When the user types "rea" after "re", we cancel the in-flight request for "re" using AbortController. This prevents the stale response from overwriting the fresh one. The pattern uses a ref to store the current controller:

const abortControllerRef = useRef(null);

async function fetchSuggestions(query) {
  // Cancel previous request
  if (abortControllerRef.current) {
    abortControllerRef.current.abort();
  }
  // Create new controller
  const controller = new AbortController();
  abortControllerRef.current = controller;

  try {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/suggest?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`, {
      signal: controller.signal,
    });
    const data = await response.json();
    // Only update if this request wasn't aborted
    if (!controller.signal.aborted) {
      setSuggestions(data);
    }
  } catch (error) {
    if (error.name !== 'AbortError') {
      // Handle real errors (network failure, 500)
      setError('Failed to load suggestions');
    }
  }
}

This reduces stale response races to near-zero. However, a race remains if two requests complete simultaneously (e.g., both from HTTP cache) — the last setState wins, potentially showing wrong data. Add a request ID guard as a second layer.

Request Sequencing — The Final Guard

Tag each request with an incrementing ID. In the response handler, only call setState if the response's ID matches the latest dispatched ID:

const latestRequestId = useRef(0);

async function fetchSuggestions(query) {
  const requestId = ++latestRequestId.current;
  // ... fetch logic ...
  const data = await response.json();
  if (requestId === latestRequestId.current) {
    setSuggestions(data);
  }
}

This eliminates the simultaneous-response race. Combined with debounce and AbortController, you have a three-layer defense: debounce reduces volume, AbortController cancels stale requests, and request sequencing ensures only the latest response updates state.

Caching and Performance Optimization

Cache results in a Map<string, Suggestion[]> keyed by query prefix. For a 1000-entry cache, memory usage is ~50–100 KB. Use an LRU eviction policy to cap size at 500 entries. Cache hit rate for repeated queries (e.g., "ap", "app", "appl") is ~40–60%, reducing API calls by that amount. Implement cache-first, network-fallback: check cache before fetching, and update cache on response. For stale-while-revalidate, serve cached data immediately and refresh in background.

⚠ Common Pitfall

Using useEffect with query as a dependency without cleanup. If the component unmounts before the fetch completes, React warns about state updates on unmounted components. Always use the cleanup function to abort the request: return () => controller.abort().

Senior signal: For high-traffic autocomplete (e.g., Google Search), serve suggestions from a Bloom filter at the edge — a probabilistic data structure that checks if a prefix exists in the index with zero false negatives and configurable false positive rate (e.g., 1%). This avoids a cache miss on non-existent prefixes, reducing backend load by 30–50%.
🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1How does AbortController interact with HTTP/2 multiplexing — can it cancel a single stream without affecting others?
    Yes, AbortController maps to RST_STREAM in HTTP/2, which cancels only that stream without closing the TCP connection. The browser sends a RST_STREAM frame to the server, which stops processing the request. This is efficient — other streams (e.g., for other tabs) continue unaffected. In HTTP/1.1, aborting closes the entire connection, causing a new TCP handshake for subsequent requests (~1 RTT penalty).
  2. 2What happens if the user types faster than the debounce timer — how do you avoid request pile-up?
    With a 300 ms debounce, if the user types 5 characters in 200 ms, only one request fires (for the final character). The timer resets on each keystroke, so intermediate characters never trigger a request. This prevents pile-up. However, if the user pauses for 300 ms after each character, you get one request per character — that's fine. The risk is if the server is slow (e.g., 500 ms) and the user types quickly after a pause — you may have two concurrent requests. AbortController handles this by cancelling the first.
  3. 3How do you handle race conditions when the autocomplete uses WebSocket instead of HTTP?
    WebSocket has no built-in request cancellation. Use a request ID in each message: send { id: 1, query: "re" }, then { id: 2, query: "rea" }. The server processes both but includes the ID in the response. The client discards responses with IDs older than the latest sent. This is the request sequencing pattern. Additionally, the server can skip processing if it receives a newer request for the same session — implement a server-side latest-request-ID check.
  4. 4How would you design a client-side autocomplete for 100,000 items with sub-10 ms response time?
    Pre-build a Trie (prefix tree) from the dataset. Each node stores the prefix and a sorted list of top-5 suggestions by frequency. Memory: ~2 MB for 100k items (assuming average string length 15). Search is O(k) where k is query length — typically <1 ms for k=10. Use a Web Worker to avoid blocking the main thread. For fuzzy matching, add a Levenshtein automaton that traverses the Trie with edit distance 1 — adds ~5 ms for a 5-character query.
  5. 5How do you monitor and alert on autocomplete race conditions in production?
    Log a race_condition metric when the request ID guard discards a response (i.e., response ID < latestRequestId). Track the rate per session and per user. Set an alert if the rate exceeds 5% of total requests — this indicates the AbortController is failing (e.g., due to HTTP cache returning responses instantly). Also monitor abort_rate (requests aborted vs total) — a rate below 10% suggests debounce is too aggressive; above 50% suggests debounce is too loose. Use distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) to correlate client-side race events with server-side request processing.

question: How would you design an infinite scrolling image gallery for optimal performance?
expectedPoints: Explain how to implement infinite scrolling efficiently.
Discuss strategies to maintain 60fps smooth scrolling.
Describe methods to manage memory and prevent leaks.
Explain how to optimize data usage on mobile devices.
Discuss handling large image datasets without performance degradation.
followUps: How would you handle image caching to improve performance?
What techniques would you use to ensure smooth transitions between images?
childExplanation: Imagine you have a huge book with lots of pictures. You want to look at the pictures one by one without the book getting too heavy or slow. You need to find a way to see each picture quickly and smoothly, even if there are thousands of them.
detailedExplanation:
Intersection Observer — The Scroll Trigger

The core of infinite scroll is detecting when the user approaches the bottom of the current content. Use the IntersectionObserver API instead of scroll event listeners for better performance (no main-thread layout thrashing). Place a sentinel element (a 1px tall <div>) at the bottom of the list. When it enters the viewport, trigger the next page load.

const sentinelRef = useRef(null);
const [page, setPage] = useState(1);

useEffect(() => {
  const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
    ([entry]) => {
      if (entry.isIntersecting && !loading && hasMore) {
        setPage((p) => p + 1);
      }
    },
    { rootMargin: "200px" } // trigger 200px before visible
  );
  if (sentinelRef.current) observer.observe(sentinelRef.current);
  return () => observer.disconnect();
}, [loading, hasMore]);

Key tuning: rootMargin of 200–400px gives the network request time to complete before the user reaches the bottom. On mobile with 60fps scrolling, this avoids visible loading jank. The observer fires at most once per frame, costing ~0.1ms per check vs. scroll handlers that can fire 100+ times per frame.

Data Fetching & Pagination Strategy

Use cursor-based pagination (e.g., ?after=nextCursor123) over offset-based (?page=2&limit=20) to avoid duplicates when new items are inserted at the top. The API response should include:

  • items: array of content objects (~20–50 items per page for mobile; keep payload under 50KB uncompressed)
  • nextCursor: opaque string for the next page, or null when exhausted
  • hasMore: boolean (redundant with cursor but avoids a null check)

Implement a request deduplication layer: if the user scrolls past the sentinel twice before the first response arrives, only one request fires. Use a loadingRef (not state) to avoid stale closures:

const loadingRef = useRef(false);
async function fetchNextPage() {
  if (loadingRef.current) return;
  loadingRef.current = true;
  try {
    const res = await fetch(`/api/feed?cursor=${cursorRef.current}`);
    const data = await res.json();
    setItems((prev) => [...prev, ...data.items]);
    cursorRef.current = data.nextCursor;
    setHasMore(data.hasMore);
  } finally {
    loadingRef.current = false;
  }
}

For mobile networks (3G: ~400ms RTT, 1.5 Mbps), compress responses with Brotli (saves 20–30% over gzip). Target P95 load time of each page under 800ms from trigger to render.

Virtualisation — Don't Render What's Off-Screen

Infinite scroll without virtualisation will crash the browser after ~500 items (each item ~200px tall = 100,000px DOM). Use a virtualised list library (e.g., react-window or @tanstack/react-virtual) that only renders ~3x the viewport height of items (typically 15–30 items on mobile).

Implementation details:

  • Fixed-size items: use FixedSizeList with itemSize set to the average item height (e.g., 180px for a card). Measure actual height on first render with ResizeObserver and adjust.
  • Variable-size items: use VariableSizeList with a itemSize callback. Pre-calculate heights from content length (e.g., text length / 80 chars per line * 20px line height).
  • Overscan: render 5 extra items above and below the visible window to prevent blank flashes during fast scroll.

Memory impact: 30 DOM nodes vs. 500+ nodes reduces layout cost by ~95%. Each re-render of the virtualised list takes <5ms on modern devices.

Error Handling & Retry Logic

Mobile networks are unreliable. Implement a retry with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, max 3 retries). Show a subtle inline error indicator (e.g., a small "Tap to retry" button) rather than a full-screen error. Use navigator.onLine and the online/offline events to pause/resume fetching:

useEffect(() => {
  const handleOnline = () => { setOnline(true); };
  const handleOffline = () => { setOnline(false); };
  window.addEventListener("online", handleOnline);
  window.addEventListener("offline", handleOffline);
  return () => {
    window.removeEventListener("online", handleOnline);
    window.removeEventListener("offline", handleOffline);
  };
}, []);

For offline support, cache the last 3 pages in IndexedDB (via idb-keyval or Dexie.js) so the user can scroll through previously loaded content without network. On reconnection, resume from the last successful cursor.

⚠ Common Pitfall

Not handling the "empty state" when the API returns zero items after the first page. This causes the sentinel to keep triggering, resulting in infinite retries. Always check hasMore before fetching, and if the response has items.length === 0, set hasMore = false immediately.

Senior signal: On mobile, consider scroll-anchoring — when new items load above the current viewport (e.g., a live feed), the browser may jump the user's position. Use overflow-anchor: auto on the scroll container to prevent this. For React, use a getBoundingClientRect-based anchor to the first visible item's ID and restore scroll position after new items are prepended.
🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1How does the IntersectionObserver callback interact with React's batching — what edge case arises?
    The observer callback runs outside React's synthetic event system. If you call setState inside it, React 17 will trigger a synchronous re-render (no batching). In React 18+, startTransition or flushSync can control batching. The edge case: if the observer fires twice in quick succession (e.g., fast scroll past sentinel), two setPage calls may cause two renders. Use unstable_batchedUpdates (React 17) or wrap in ReactDOM.flushSync to batch.
  2. 2How do you prevent duplicate items when the user scrolls back up and then down again?
    Use a Set of item IDs to deduplicate on insertion. When new items arrive from the API, filter out any IDs already in the set before appending. Store the set in a useRef to avoid re-renders. For cursor-based pagination, the cursor ensures no overlap, but network retries or race conditions can still produce duplicates. The set check is a cheap O(1) guard per item.
  3. 3What happens when the user scrolls extremely fast — how do you handle the "blank gap" problem?
    Fast scroll can outpace the fetch, leaving a blank area below the last loaded item. Solution: increase rootMargin to 800px (pre-fetch earlier) and use a staggered loading pattern — load 2 pages ahead. The virtualised list's overscanCount should be set to 10+ items. Also, use scroll-snap-type: y mandatory on the container to slow down the scroll gesture, giving the network more time.
  4. 4How do you handle memory pressure when the user scrolls through 10,000 items?
    Virtualisation only handles DOM nodes, not the data array. The items array grows unboundedly. Implement a windowed data buffer: keep only the last 500 items in memory, discard items scrolled past (store their cursors for potential back-scroll). Use useRef for the buffer and only slice the visible range for rendering. For images, use loading="lazy" and IntersectionObserver to unload off-screen images (set src to empty string).
  5. 5How would you add analytics to measure scroll depth and content engagement?
    Track scrollDepth as a percentage of total content loaded (e.g., 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%). Use a IntersectionObserver on marker elements at each depth threshold. For engagement, log itemImpression events when an item enters the viewport (debounced to 200ms) and itemViewTime (time between impression and scroll-away). Batch these events and send every 5 seconds or 20 events, whichever comes first, to reduce network overhead. Use sendBeacon for the final batch on page unload.

question: How would you design an infinite data table for large datasets?
expectedPoints: Distinguishes window virtualisation (fixed row heights) from dynamic virtualisation (measured heights) and knows when each applies.
Implements cursor-based pagination for fetching rows; explains why offset pagination fails at scale.
Handles bi-directional scroll: prepend rows when scrolling up without losing scroll position.
Designs sticky headers, column resizing, and column sorting without re-fetching the full dataset.
Addresses accessibility: data table ARIA roles (role=grid, rowheader, columnheader, aria-sort).
Discusses performance budget: 60 fps scroll requires DOM node count < ~500 rendered at any time.
followUps: How do you measure and cache variable row heights for a virtualised list?
What is the difference between react-window and tanstack/virtual — when would you pick each?
How would you implement column sorting on a 10M-row server-side dataset?
How do you handle keyboard navigation across thousands of rows (PgDown, Ctrl+End)?
How would you add inline cell editing to a virtualised table without losing scroll context?
How do you keep the table state (selected rows, scroll position) when navigating away and back?
childExplanation: Imagine a giant library with millions of books. Instead of showing all the books at once, you only show the ones near you as you move around. This helps you find books faster without getting overwhelmed.
detailedExplanation:
Interview Framework

Clarify: row count order of magnitude (10k, 1M, 10M)? Row height: fixed or variable? Server-side or client-side sort/filter? Editable cells? Then structure: virtualisation strategy → data fetching → scroll management → sorting/filtering → accessibility.

Why Virtualisation is Mandatory

Rendering 100k rows as real DOM nodes is catastrophic: initial paint can take 10+ seconds, scrolling drops below 5 fps, memory usage spikes to gigabytes. The solution: only render the ~20–40 rows visible in the viewport plus an overscan buffer of ~5 rows above/below. As the user scrolls, recycle and reposition a fixed pool of DOM nodes — total DOM nodes stays ~50 regardless of data size.

Fixed vs Dynamic Height Virtualisation

  • Fixed row height (simplest): each row is exactly N px. Total scroll height = rowCount × rowHeight. Start index = Math.floor(scrollTop / rowHeight). react-window's FixedSizeList handles this out-of-the-box.
  • Dynamic row height: rows contain multi-line text, images, or expandable content. Approach: measure rendered height via ResizeObserver, cache in a Map<rowIndex, number>, and maintain a prefix-sum array for O(log n) scroll offset → row index lookup. @tanstack/virtual supports this natively via measureElement.

Data Fetching — Cursor vs Offset Pagination

Offset pagination (LIMIT 100 OFFSET 5000) is simple but fails at scale: the DB must scan 5,000 rows to skip them, and inserting rows above offset N shifts everything below — causing duplicates or gaps on next page.

Cursor-based (WHERE id > :cursor ORDER BY id LIMIT 100): O(1) seek via index, stable across inserts. The response includes a nextCursor token for the next page. Maintain a page cache per cursor window — once fetched, cache in memory so reverse scrolling doesn't refetch.

Bi-Directional Scroll Without Layout Jump

When the user scrolls back to the top and you prepend new rows, the scroll container jumps because the total height grew above the viewport. Fix: read scrollTop before the DOM update, calculate the height of prepended rows, then set scrollTop += prependedHeight after the update. CSS overflow-anchor: none disables the browser's built-in scroll anchoring so you control it manually.

⚠ Common Pitfall

Triggering a fetch on every scroll event. Instead, use an IntersectionObserver on a sentinel element placed N rows before the end of the loaded data. Fetch the next page only when the sentinel enters the viewport — debounced, not per-pixel scroll.

Sorting and Filtering at Scale

  • Server-side (recommended for >50k rows): send sort column and direction in the API request. Invalidate and refetch from cursor 0 on sort change.
  • Column sort indicator: aria-sort="ascending" / "descending" / "none" on <th> elements.
  • Multi-column sort: maintain an ordered list of { column, direction } tuples. Show sort priority numbers in column headers.

Accessibility

Use role="grid" (interactive) or role="table" (read-only) on the container. Each row: role="row". Header cells: role="columnheader". Data cells: role="gridcell". Keyboard navigation: Arrow keys move between cells, Page Down/Up scroll by viewport height, Ctrl+End jumps to last loaded row.

Senior signal: cite the target metric — 60 fps scroll requires keeping the main thread under 16 ms per frame. Profile with Chrome DevTools Rendering tab; look for "Recalculate Style" and "Layout" thrash caused by reading offsetHeight in a loop.
🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1How do you compute the correct scrollTop offset for the virtualised list when row heights are variable?
    Maintain a prefix-sum array: offsets[i] is the cumulative height of rows 0 through i-1. Total scroll height = offsets[rowCount]. To find which row is at scrollTop: binary search on offsets — O(log n). To compute row i's top CSS position: offsets[i]. When row heights change: update the measured height in the cache, recompute the prefix-sum from that index forward. @tanstack/virtual's measureElement callback handles this automatically via ResizeObserver.
  2. 2How do you implement row selection (checkboxes) that persists while rows are virtualised and recycled?
    Store selection state in a Set<rowId> outside the virtualised list (in parent component state or a store). When a row DOM node is recycled to display a different row index, it reads from this external set to determine its checked state. This decouples visual state from DOM identity. For "select all": optimise as an "all except" set: store { mode: "all", excluded: Set<rowId> } instead of a potentially enormous "all included" set.
  3. 3Why does offset pagination break at large offsets and how exactly does cursor pagination fix it?
    SELECT * FROM rows ORDER BY id LIMIT 100 OFFSET 50000 forces the database to read and discard 50,000 rows before returning the 100 you want — even with an index, this is an O(offset) operation. Cursor pagination: SELECT * FROM rows WHERE id > :lastId ORDER BY id LIMIT 100 uses the B-tree index to seek directly to lastId in O(log n), then reads the next 100 rows. Zero wasted work. Cursor also handles concurrent inserts: a new row above the current cursor doesn't shift the cursor position, so no duplicates or skipped rows on the next page.
  4. 4How do you handle column resizing in a virtualised table without layout thrash?
    Avoid per-cell width reads during a drag (layout thrash). Instead: on drag start, snapshot all column widths into a JS object. On pointermove, compute new width = snapshotWidth + deltaX and update a CSS custom property: --col-{id}-width: {width}px. Each cell uses width: var(--col-{id}-width). CSS variable updates are batched by the browser and don't trigger synchronous layout. On pointerup, persist the widths to state. This keeps the resize handler at 60 fps with zero layout invalidation during drag.
  5. 5How do you restore scroll position when the user navigates away and back?
    Save scroll state to the router history entry (via history.replaceState or a navigation store). Store: { scrollTop, loadedPages, filters, sortState }. On mount: if history entry has saved state, restore scrollTop after the first render cycle (in a useLayoutEffect to avoid flash). Re-hydrate the data cache with the saved pages so the user doesn't see a blank table while refetching. For SPA navigation, keep the table component mounted (CSS hide/show) to avoid teardown/re-init cost entirely — valid for performance-critical tables.
