question: How would you design a PWA with reliable offline support, app installability, and push notifications — covering the service worker lifecycle and iOS/Android platform differences?
expectedPoints: Explains service worker lifecycle (install, activate, fetch) and uses skipWaiting/clients.claim correctly.
Describes caching strategies (cache-first for static, network-first for API) and handles offline fallback.
Covers Web App Manifest requirements and platform-specific install prompts (beforeinstallprompt vs iOS banner).
Details Web Push API flow: permission, subscription, VAPID, push event, notification display.
Identifies iOS limitations (no background sync, aggressive SW killing, missing notification features) and proposes workarounds.
followUps: How would you implement a retry queue for failed API calls when the user goes offline?
What are the security considerations for push notifications (e.g., payload encryption, VAPID)?
How do you test a PWA offline on iOS Safari given its restrictions?
childExplanation: Imagine you have a magic coloring book that works even when you lose your crayons, and it can tap you on the shoulder when it's time to color. That's what a PWA does: it saves your app so it works without internet, can be added to your phone's home screen like a real app, and can send you reminders even when the app is closed.
detailedExplanation:
Service Worker Lifecycle & Offline Support

A service worker (SW) is a JavaScript file that runs in the background, separate from the web page. Its lifecycle consists of: install, activate, and fetch events. During install, we pre-cache critical assets (HTML, CSS, JS, fonts) using the Cache API. The SW waits for activation until all tabs are closed, but we can call self.skipWaiting() to force activation. In activate, we clean old caches. The fetch event intercepts network requests; we implement a cache-first strategy for static assets and a network-first strategy for API calls, falling back to cached responses or an offline page.

// Service Worker: install event with pre-caching
self.addEventListener('install', event => {
  event.waitUntil(
    caches.open('v1').then(cache => {
      return cache.addAll([
        '/',
        '/styles/main.css',
        '/scripts/app.js',
        '/offline.html'
      ]);
    })
  );
  self.skipWaiting();
});

self.addEventListener('fetch', event => {
  event.respondWith(
    caches.match(event.request).then(cached => {
      return cached || fetch(event.request).catch(() => caches.match('/offline.html'));
    })
  );
});

For dynamic content, use a network-first strategy with a timeout (e.g., 3s). If the network fails, serve the last cached version. This improves perceived performance and reliability.

⚠ Common Pitfall

Developers often forget to handle fetch for opaque responses (e.g., CDN resources). These have status 0 and cannot be read in JS. Always check response.type !== 'opaque' before caching, or use a no-cors mode.

Installability: Web App Manifest & Criteria

Installability requires a manifest.json with at least: name, short_name, start_url, display: 'standalone', icons (192px and 512px), and a registered SW with a fetch handler. On Android, Chrome prompts the user to install; on iOS, Safari supports 'Add to Home Screen' but not the beforeinstallprompt event. To trigger install on Android, listen for beforeinstallprompt and call prompt() after user interaction. On iOS, you must guide users via a custom banner.

// Trigger install prompt on Android
let deferredPrompt;
window.addEventListener('beforeinstallprompt', (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  deferredPrompt = e;
  // Show install button
  installBtn.style.display = 'block';
  installBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
    deferredPrompt.prompt();
    deferredPrompt.userChoice.then(choice => {
      if (choice.outcome === 'accepted') { /* installed */ }
      deferredPrompt = null;
    });
  });
});

On iOS, the manifest is supported but the install prompt is not. Instead, Safari shows a share sheet with 'Add to Home Screen'. Developers can detect standalone mode via window.navigator.standalone (iOS) or matchMedia('(display-mode: standalone)').

Push Notifications: Web Push API & Permission

Push notifications require: 1) User permission via Notification.requestPermission(), 2) Subscribing to push via registration.pushManager.subscribe() with a VAPID public key, 3) Sending the subscription object to the server. The server sends push messages using the Web Push Protocol (RFC 8030). The SW listens for push event, parses payload, and calls self.registration.showNotification(). On Android, notifications appear; on iOS, Safari supports push since iOS 16.4 but requires the app to be added to the home screen and the user to grant permission via a native prompt.

// Service Worker: push event
self.addEventListener('push', event => {
  const data = event.data.json();
  const options = {
    body: data.body,
    icon: '/icon-192.png',
    badge: '/badge-72.png',
    data: { url: data.url }
  };
  event.waitUntil(
    self.registration.showNotification(data.title, options)
  );
});

// Notification click
self.addEventListener('notificationclick', event => {
  event.notification.close();
  event.waitUntil(
    clients.openWindow(event.notification.data.url)
  );
});

On iOS, push notifications require the app to be added to the home screen and the user to accept the permission dialog. The SW must be registered and active. Note that iOS does not support badge or vibrate in notifications.

Platform Differences: iOS vs Android

  • Service Worker Lifecycle: On iOS, SWs are killed more aggressively; use self.skipWaiting() and clients.claim() to take control immediately. On Android, SWs persist longer.
  • Cache Storage: iOS has a 50MB limit per origin (shared with other storage). Android has no fixed limit but may evict under pressure. Use navigator.storage.estimate() to check.
  • Push Notifications: iOS requires the app to be added to the home screen and user permission; no vibrate or badge support. Android supports all features.
  • Install Prompt: Android has beforeinstallprompt; iOS does not. On iOS, guide users via a custom banner.
  • Background Sync: iOS does not support the Background Sync API; use setTimeout or IndexedDB with retry logic.
Senior signal: The key to reliable offline is not just caching but also handling stale data. Use a cache-first strategy for UI assets, but for data, implement a stale-while-revalidate pattern with a background sync (if available) or a retry queue in IndexedDB. On iOS, since Background Sync is missing, you must rely on the fetch event to attempt revalidation on every request.
🪜 Deep Dive Ladder — Self-Interview

Answer before expanding.

  1. 1How does the service worker lifecycle work, and how do you control when a new SW takes effect?
    The SW lifecycle has install, waiting, activate, and redundant states. After install, the SW waits until all tabs are closed. To skip waiting, call self.skipWaiting() during install. In activate, call clients.claim() to take control of uncontrolled clients. This ensures the new SW handles all fetches immediately.
  2. 2How do you implement a cache-first strategy for static assets and a network-first strategy for API calls?
    In the fetch event, check the request URL or headers. For static assets (e.g., images, CSS), respond with caches.match(request) first; if not found, fetch and cache. For API calls, try network first; if it fails, serve cached response. Use a timeout (e.g., 3s) to avoid hanging. Cache API responses with a separate cache name for easy invalidation.
  3. 3What are the edge cases when serving cached content offline, especially for dynamic data?
    Stale data can mislead users. Implement a stale-while-revalidate pattern: serve cached data immediately, then fetch updated data in the background and update the cache. For POST requests, cache only if idempotent. Handle opaque responses (status 0) by not caching them. Use IndexedDB to store a queue of failed mutations and retry when online.
  4. 4How do you handle push notifications on iOS given the platform limitations?
    On iOS, push requires the app to be added to the home screen and user permission. The SW must be registered and active. Use VAPID for authentication. Note that badge and vibrate are not supported. For notification click, use clients.openWindow. Since iOS may kill the SW, consider using navigator.serviceWorker.ready to ensure registration.
  5. 5How do you ensure backward compatibility and graceful degradation for browsers that don't support SW or push?
    Check for SW support before registering: if ('serviceWorker' in navigator). For push, check 'PushManager' in window. If unsupported, fall back to standard HTTP caching (Cache-Control headers) and polling for updates. Use feature detection to hide install prompts. For notifications, use a fallback UI (e.g., in-app notification center). Always test on multiple browsers.
